standing_assumptions:
The article is Carlson, Incerti and Aronow, ‘Dyadic Clustering in International Relations’, Political Analysis 32:186–198 (2024). Printed page = PDF page + 185 (printed p. 191 is PDF p. 6). Everything quoted below and in the targets was read from the rendered page images (staged/pages/p-NN.png and the publisher-supplement page images, checked against 170–220 dpi renderings of staged/main.pdf and of the supplement). The paper has no numbered theorem, proposition, lemma or equation; its formal content is two displays in Section 2.1, the sandwich displays and the decomposition display in Section 3, and Tables 2–4. It writes $\mathrm{V}[\cdot]$ for variance, $\mathrm{E}[\cdot]$ for expectation and a superscript $T$ for transpose.
(S1) Model, p. 189 (PDF p. 4), Section 3: “To ease exposition, we consider the linear model of $Y_{ijt}$ on regressors $x_{ijt}$, $$Y_{ijt} = \beta x_{ijt} + u_{ijt},$$ where $Y_{ijt}$ is the level of commerce between countries $i$ and $j$ in time period or observation $t$ and $\beta$ is the slope that we obtain from fitting this model to the entire population. Under the exogeneity condition $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}\,|\,x_{ijt}] = 0$ and the usual regularity conditions, the parameters of this model can be estimated using ordinary least squares.”
(S2) Sandwich and plug-in estimator, p. 189: “Generically, the variance of an estimated parameter from a linear model can be represented in a symmetric form that resembles a sandwich, with two identical “bread” matrices and a “meat” matrix multiplied together in the order of bread, meat, and bread again (Aronow and Miller 2019; Davidson and MacKinnon 2004; Greene 2002): $$V_{sandwich} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\Omega X(X^TX)^{-1},$$ where $X$ denotes the matrix of regressors, and $\Omega$ is the variance–covariance matrix of model errors, such that $\Omega_{ijt,i'j't'} = \mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}]$. Robust sandwich estimators are formed by assuming that some elements of $\Omega$ are equal to zero, and then substituting residuals for errors, and means for expectations. Thus, the empirical variance–covariance matrix of model residuals, $\hat\Omega$, can be plugged into the above expression of variance to arrive at a variance estimator of the following form:$^1$ $$\hat V = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\hat\Omega X(X^TX)^{-1}.$$ So long as there is not “too much” clustering (for a precise statement, see Aronow, Crawford, and Zubizarreta 2018), $\hat V$ will be a consistent estimator of the variance–covariance matrix of the sampling distribution of $\hat\beta$.” Footnote 1: “Both the Eicker–Huber–White heteroskedasticity-consistent variance estimator and the Liang and Zeger cluster robust variance estimator are sandwich-like, “plug-in” variance estimators of this form, each making differing assumptions about $\Omega$.”
(S3) The three restrictions on $\Omega$, pp. 189–190 (PDF pp. 4–5). Naive: “The simplest case is to assume that there is no dependence across observations whatsoever in the data, which is the assumption for non-clustered RSEs: if $i \ne i'$, $j \ne j'$, **or** $t \ne t'$, then $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}] = 0$, or that the errors are uncorrelated.” (Table 2; ‘or’ is bold in the paper). Repeated dyad: “The most common approach is clustering by dyad, where it is assumed that errors are correlated when $i = i'$ and $j = j'$, regardless of time period.” and “all observations in the matrix of model errors that do not share both members of the dyad are still assumed to be uncorrelated (i.e., $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}] = 0$).” (Table 3). Dyadic: “By contrast, our approach only assumes independence when country pairs share no members.” and “In the matrix shown in Table 4—full dyadic clustering—we can now see that the only observations assumed to be independent are those for which the dyad does not share any members with other observations.” Tables 2–4 (p. 190) display the three patterns for six observations labelled $ijt = 111, 112, 211, 212, 221, 222$, with entries $\mathrm{E}[u_{ijt}u_{i'j't'}]$ or 0: Table 2 is diagonal; Table 3 has the three blocks $\{111,112\}$, $\{211,212\}$, $\{221,222\}$; Table 4 is zero only between $\{111,112\}$ and $\{221,222\}$.
(S4) Decomposition and DCRSEs, pp. 190–191 (PDF pp. 5–6): the display $\hat V_r = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat V_{c,i} - \hat V_D - (N-2)\hat V_0$, the sentence defining its four terms and footnotes 2 and 3 are quoted in full in P032-T11.
(S5) Reanalysis conventions, p. 192 (PDF p. 7), the last sentence running onto p. 193: “For the purposes of our reanalysis, dyads are assumed to be undirected, as modeling dyadic clustering based on directed dyads would require a stronger assumption about independence across observations.$^{11}$ Also, for the purposes of our primary reanalysis, there are no small-sample corrections made to our standard error estimates.” $N$ is not defined beside the display on p. 191; the note to Supplementary Table A.5 (supplement p. A5) says: “$N$ is the number of unique dyad members in the analytic sample.”
(S6) Terms. p. 187 (PDF p. 2): “non-incident dyads (i.e., dyads that do not share a common member)”; two observations are called incident here when their dyads share a member. KEV, p. 192: “KEVs are defined as independent variables whose parameter estimates are directly referenced in the study, or otherwise clearly pertain to the study’s stated hypotheses.” SER, p. 193 (PDF p. 8): “We compute a standard error ratio (SER) for all KEVs, which is the DCRSE divided by the standard error produced using the original variance estimation strategy.” ISFW, p. 193 and footnote 14: “where “study frequency” is the total number of KEVs for a given study appearing in the analytic sample” and “ISFW is equivalent to an average of averages across studies.”
(S7) Not in the paper. The targets index observations (records) by a single index $r$ with an unordered dyad $d_r$ of two distinct members, write $z_r$ for the bread-premultiplied score of record $r$, and call a sandwich ‘unadjusted’ when it carries no finite-sample factor. These conventions are the validators’ and are flagged where used. Every target is an exact finite statement; the two limits quoted in P032-T1 are consequences of exact identities stated there.
(S8) Which findings are targets. Of the sixteen findings rated error, five have a mathematical statement to correct or rest on an exact formal counterexample: P032-E001 (Moderate; the direction of the effect of dependence between non-incident dyads), P032-N004 (Moderate; the matrix subtracted in the decomposition for survival data), P032-E005 (Minor; the positive-semidefinite option), P032-N012 (Minor; finite-sample factors applied to Rubin-pooled matrices) and P032-E002 (Minor; a count against Supplementary Table A.2, for which the validator’s evidence is itself a Lean proof). The other eleven are not targets because their corrections change no mathematical statement: P032-E004 (an unreachable branch of the Stata command), P032-E006 (row alignment and dyad labels in the R package), P032-E008 (a selector typo that drops two KEVs; 693 for 691), P032-E009 (Supplementary Table A.3 built from the wrong result files), P032-E010 (the description of point area in Figure 3), P032-E011 (the small-sample rerun of the original standard errors), P032-N006 (the classification of Shelef 2016 as having fixed effects for both dyad members), P032-N010 (minimum Stata version), P032-N011 (an observation count in Supplementary Table A.1), P032-E003 (a cross-reference) and P032-E012 (a reference year). Of the eleven headline claims, P032-H7 (the decomposition identity), P032-H9 (the toy-example variance) and P032-H10 (the lower-bound claim, refuted by P032-E001) contain a mathematical statement; the others are empirical estimates, counts or interpretive remarks.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The decomposition as it must be implemented, with every hypothesis: record-level $\hat V_0$ and common scores, bread and scaling in all components; and the exact discrepancy when an id-clustered matrix is subtracted instead
canonical_claim.location: p. 191 (PDF p. 6), display for $\hat V_r$ and the sentence defining its terms; dcr.ado lines 108–119 and 163–190
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol’s smallest repair (validated.json, P032-N004), verbatim: “Compute the subtraction covariance using an explicit cluster variable unique to each estimation-sample record, while retaining the original stset ID, especially for stcrreg's censoring-weight calculations. Use noadjust for every sandwich component, or otherwise remove command-specific factors so all components share the same scaling, fitted contributions, bread, and sample. Rerun the affected survival fits and dependent summaries before issuing numerical corrections. This changes implementation, not the estimand or substantive assumptions.”
Formal content, with every hypothesis. Let $r = 1,\ldots,n$ index the records of the estimation sample; let $\mathcal{M}$ be a finite set of members with $|\mathcal{M}| = N$; let each record have an unordered dyad $d_r = \{a_r,b_r\}\subseteq\mathcal{M}$ with $a_r\ne b_r$; and let $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb{R}^p$ be arbitrary vectors (the bread-premultiplied score of each record; the same vectors in every component). Define the sandwich sums without finite-sample factors $$V_0 = \sum_rz_rz_r^T,\qquad V_D = \sum_{r,s:\,d_r=d_s}z_rz_s^T,\qquad V_{c,i} = \sum_{r,s:\,i\in d_r\cap d_s}z_rz_s^T + \sum_{r:\,i\notin d_r}z_rz_r^T\ \ (i\in\mathcal{M}),\qquad V_{DCR} = \sum_{r,s:\,d_r\cap d_s\ne\emptyset}z_rz_s^T,$$ the double sums being over ordered pairs of records.
(i) [The decomposition] $\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}V_{c,i} - V_D - (N-2)V_0 = V_{DCR}$.
(ii) [Coefficient count] For an ordered pair $(r,s)$ the coefficient of $z_rz_s^T$ on the left of (i) is $N - 1 - (N-2) = 1$ if $r = s$; $2 - 1 - 0 = 1$ if $r\ne s$ and $d_r = d_s$; $1 - 0 - 0 = 1$ if $d_r\ne d_s$ and $|d_r\cap d_s| = 1$; and $0$ if $d_r\cap d_s = \emptyset$. Two distinct two-member sets share zero or one member, so the cases are exhaustive.
(iii) [An id-clustered matrix subtracted instead] Let each record also carry an id $g_r$ and let $V_{id} = \sum_{r,s:\,g_r=g_s}z_rz_s^T$. Then $$\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}V_{c,i} - V_D - (N-2)V_{id} = V_{DCR} + (N-2)(V_0 - V_{id}) = V_{DCR} - (N-2)\sum_{r\ne s:\,g_r=g_s}z_rz_s^T.$$ The left side equals $V_{DCR}$ when every id has a single record; in general it does not (P032-T3).
(iv) [With a residual finite-sample factor] If the matrix subtracted is $\alpha V_{id}$ for a real $\alpha$ (under the ‘asylike’ option, $\alpha = \frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\frac{g}{g-1}$ with $g$ the number of ids), the result is $V_{DCR} + (N-2)(V_0 - \alpha V_{id})$.
(v) [Corrected implementation] Subtracting $(N-2)$ times the record-level matrix $V_0$ (each estimation-sample record its own cluster, with the same scores, bread and scaling as the other components) returns $V_{DCR}$, by (i).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As printed: P032-T11 (the display; the definitions of $\hat V_r$, $\hat V_{c,i}$, $\hat V_D$, $\hat V_0$; footnote 2). $V_{DCR}$ is the paper’s $\hat V_r$ written as a sum over pairs of records (the plug-in estimator of (S2) under the pattern of Table 4). $N$: (S5); (i) holds for any finite $\mathcal{M}$ containing every member that occurs (a member with no record has $V_{c,i} = V_0$). That every record outside member $i$’s cluster is its own cluster is not stated in the paper: it is the validators’ reading (P032-N005, a clarity note) and what dcr.ado does (lines 108–119). $z_r$, $V_{id}$, $g_r$ and $\alpha$ are the validators’ symbols. For least squares $z_r = (X^TX)^{-1}x_r\hat u_r$ with $x_r$ the $r$-th row of $X$ as a column; the identity is algebraic and holds for any vectors $z_r$.
canonical_claim.note: Corrected statement for P032-N004 (error, Moderate). Repair cost per the validators: none in the mathematics (same estimand and assumptions); an implementation change and a re-run of the 13 survival models before any numerical correction is issued. (i)–(ii) are the adjudicating validator’s universal proof (proof.md, section 2) and are the headline identity P032-T11 with its hypotheses made explicit; (iii)–(iv) are its conditional discrepancy (section 3), stated there for the unprojected matrix, before the eigenvalue step of footnote 3. (i) needs two distinct members per dyad: for two distinct records of a ‘dyad’ $\{i,i\}$ the coefficient is $1 - 1 - 0 = 0$ instead of 1 (P032-N003, a clarity note on the labels of Tables 2–4). What Stata returns in the cited calls is supported by the manual entries cited in settled.json, not by an execution.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The passages on pp. 187, 191 and 196 about dependence between non-incident dyads, corrected: the exact difference between the variance of a coefficient under the full error covariance and under the dyadic restriction, and the sign condition under which the dyadic value is a weak or strict lower bound
canonical_claim.location: p. 187 (PDF p. 2), paragraph beginning ‘Note, however’; p. 191 (PDF p. 6), paragraph beginning ‘Note that the above approach’; p. 196 (PDF p. 11), Conclusion, first and third paragraphs
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol’s smallest repair (validated.json, P032-E001), verbatim: “Replace 'will still underestimate' by 'may underestimate'; remove the unconditional lower-bound descriptions on pp. 187 and 196 and describe the reanalysis as a comparison of DCRSEs with the original standard errors. State that further dependence can raise or lower coefficient-specific sampling variance. Qualify the p. 191 expectation of larger variance, and its nearby 'still improve' aside, by the relevant weighted covariance signs. The p. 196 'may be even more severe' sentence can remain. If a conditional population lower bound is retained, explicitly require the omitted weighted covariance sum to be nonnegative for each relevant contrast; strict underestimation requires it to be positive.”
Corrected text (validator), verbatim: “Dependence between non-incident dyads may increase or decrease coefficient-specific sampling variance relative to the dyadic covariance restriction. For a fixed full-rank design X and contrast c^T beta-hat, put h=X(X^T X)^{-1}c and let Omega_D retain covariance entries for incident observation pairs. Then Var(c^T beta-hat)-h^T Omega_D h equals the ordered sum of h_r h_s Omega_rs over non-incident pairs. A nonnegative sum gives a weak population lower bound; a positive sum gives strict population underestimation. This condition does not guarantee finite-sample ordering of residual-based variance estimates. Our reanalysis documents changes in standard errors and significance when using DCRSEs; without justified signs for the omitted contributions, it is not a lower bound on the consequences of all inadequately modeled dependence.”
Formal content, with every hypothesis. Let $X$ be a fixed real $n\times p$ matrix of full column rank, $Y = X\beta + u$ with $u$ a random vector such that $\mathrm{E}[u] = 0$ and $\Omega = \mathrm{E}[uu^T]$ is finite, $\hat\beta = (X^TX)^{-1}X^TY$, $c\in\mathbb{R}^p$ and $h = X(X^TX)^{-1}c$. Let each observation $r$ have a dyad $d_r$ (a set of two distinct members) and let $(\Omega_D)_{rs} = \Omega_{rs}\mathbf{1}\{d_r\cap d_s\ne\emptyset\}$.
(i) $c^T\hat\beta - c^T\beta = h^Tu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(c^T\hat\beta) = h^T\Omega h = c^TV_{sandwich}c$.
(ii) $$h^T\Omega h - h^T\Omega_Dh = \Delta_c := \sum_{(r,s):\,d_r\cap d_s=\emptyset}h_rh_s\Omega_{rs},$$ the sum being over ordered pairs of observations with disjoint dyads.
(iii) $h^T\Omega_Dh\le\mathrm{Var}(c^T\hat\beta)$ if and only if $\Delta_c\ge0$; $h^T\Omega_Dh < \mathrm{Var}(c^T\hat\beta)$ if and only if $\Delta_c > 0$; and $h^T\Omega_Dh > \mathrm{Var}(c^T\hat\beta)$ if and only if $\Delta_c < 0$.
(iv) The weak ordering holds for every contrast $c$ if and only if $(X^TX)^{-1}X^T(\Omega - \Omega_D)X(X^TX)^{-1}$ is positive semidefinite, equivalently if and only if $X^T(\Omega - \Omega_D)X$ is positive semidefinite.
(v) Positive semidefiniteness of $\Omega$, exogeneity and the presence of non-zero covariance between non-incident observations do not determine the sign of $\Delta_c$ (P032-T1 (a), (c), (d), (f)); nor does non-negativity of every omitted covariance $\Omega_{rs}$ (P032-T1 (b)).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S1)–(S3); $V_{sandwich}$: (S2). $\Omega_D$ is the population form of the restriction of Table 4 (zero exactly between observations whose dyads share no member). The comparison is of population sandwich values (or of the corresponding asymptotic targets under regularity); it is not a statement about every realized residual-based estimate (both validators). The printed passages being corrected: P032-T5.
canonical_claim.note: Corrected statement for P032-E001 (error, Moderate). Repair cost per both validators: weaker conclusion (the unconditional lower-bound reading is given up; the estimator and the reported comparisons are unchanged). Retaining a conditional lower bound instead requires $\Delta_c\ge0$ for each contrast compared, an assumption not established for the 22 studies, and even then orders population values, not every finite-sample estimate. Only (i)–(v) are formal targets; the sentences about what the reanalysis documents are quoted for the record. (i)–(iii) are in v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 2, and v2/artifact/derivation.md, section 2; the first form of (iv) is in v1, section 2, and the second is the same condition after multiplying on both sides by $X^TX$. The validators add that the p. 196 sentence ‘may be even more severe’ is correct as a possibility and that the p. 191 ‘we expect’ is not refuted as an empirical expectation.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3, the decomposed form of the DCR variance estimator (unnumbered display), as printed
canonical_claim.location: pp. 190–191 (PDF pp. 5–6): the sentence beginning ‘More specifically’ at the foot of p. 190, the display and the sentence defining its terms on p. 191, footnotes 2 and 3 on p. 191
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed (pp. 190–191): “More specifically, our approach to DCRSEs follows Aronow *et al.* (2015), which, in practice, allows for the DCR variance estimator to be decomposed entirely using robust variance estimators that are readily computed using popular statistical software packages.$^2$ The DCR variance estimator in this decomposed form is $$\hat V_r = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat V_{c,i} - \hat V_D - (N-2)\hat V_0,$$ where $\hat V_r$ is the estimated DCR variance–covariance matrix for longitudinal data; $\hat V_{c,i}$ is the estimated dyad-member-$i$-specific clustered variance–covariance matrix; $\hat V_D$ is the estimated repeated-dyad clustered variance–covariance matrix; and $\hat V_0$ is the estimated heteroskedasticity-consistent variance–covariance matrix. Taking the square root of the diagonal of the DCR variance–covariance matrix yields DCRSEs for all model parameters.$^3$”
Footnote 2, as printed: “This “multi-way decomposition” approach was first introduced by Cameron, Gelbach, and Miller (2011), and is based on the realization that each dyad member “is the basis of its own cluster that intersects with other units’ clusters,” and that each of those dyad-member-specific clusters can be adjusted for using conventional cluster-robust variance estimators (Aronow *et al.* 2015). DCRSEs are mathematically equivalent to multi-way clustering on (undirected) dyad-member-specific clusters, though the large number of such multi-way clusters implies important analytic and computational distinctions.”
Footnote 3, as printed: “To account for rare instances where negative parameter estimate variances arise due to non-positive semi-definite variance-covariance matrices, an “eigendecomposition of the estimated variance matrix . . . [that] converts any negative eigenvalue(s) to zero” and then reassembles the matrix to “force” positive semi-definiteness is performed, in line with suggestions from Cameron *et al.* (2011) and Cameron and Miller (2014).”
Formal reading (exact, finite sample; the reading of both readers and of the validators). Index the observations of the sample by $r = 1,\ldots,n$; observation $r$ has an unordered dyad $d_r$ of two distinct members; $N$ is the number of distinct members occurring; $X$ is the $n\times p$ matrix of regressors, of full column rank, and $\hat u$ the vector of least-squares residuals. For a symmetric 0/1 pattern $P$ on pairs of observations let $\hat V[P] = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\hat\Omega_PX(X^TX)^{-1}$ with $(\hat\Omega_P)_{rs} = P_{rs}\hat u_r\hat u_s$ (the plug-in estimator of (S2)). Put $\hat V_r = \hat V[P^{dy}]$ with $P^{dy}_{rs} = \mathbf{1}\{d_r\cap d_s\ne\emptyset\}$ (the pattern of Table 4); $\hat V_D = \hat V[P^D]$ with $P^D_{rs} = \mathbf{1}\{d_r = d_s\}$ (Table 3); $\hat V_0 = \hat V[P^0]$ with $P^0_{rs} = \mathbf{1}\{r = s\}$ (Table 2); and $\hat V_{c,i} = \hat V[P^i]$ with $P^i_{rs} = \mathbf{1}\{i\in d_r\cap d_s\} + \mathbf{1}\{r = s,\ i\notin d_r\}$ for each member $i$. Then $$\hat V_r = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat V_{c,i} - \hat V_D - (N-2)\hat V_0;$$ equivalently, $\sum_iP^i_{rs} - P^D_{rs} - (N-2)P^0_{rs} = P^{dy}_{rs}$ for all $r,s$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S1)–(S3), (S5). $N$ is not defined beside the display; ‘the number of unique dyad members in the analytic sample’ is from the note to Supplementary Table A.5 (supplement p. A5). The cluster-robust estimator for a partition of the observations is the plug-in $\hat V$ of (S2) with $\hat\Omega_{rs} = \hat u_r\hat u_s$ when $r$ and $s$ lie in the same cluster and 0 otherwise (footnote 1; (S2)). For $\hat V_{c,i}$ the partition is: all observations whose dyad contains member $i$ form one cluster, and every other observation is its own cluster. The second half is not stated in the paper; it is supplied by the validators (P032-N005) and by the released code. Dyads are unordered ((S5)) and have two distinct members ($Y_{ijt}$ is commerce between countries $i$ and $j$, (S1)). No small-sample factors ((S5)). In the notation of P032-T4, $\hat V[P] = \sum_{r,s}P_{rs}z_rz_s^T$ with $z_r = (X^TX)^{-1}x_r\hat u_r$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P032-H7, its mathematical half (the half about the R and Stata packages is not a formal statement). The identity holds as printed with the definitions above: both readers and the validators verified it (the four-case coefficient count of P032-T4 (ii); exact small designs including repeated and reversed dyads; agreement with the direct sum over pairs in 35 re-estimated models). It is also the statement as printed for P032-N004 (error, Moderate), which concerns the implementation for survival data and leaves the display correct (P032-T3, P032-T4). Two clarity notes bear on the hypotheses and are not errors: P032-N005 ($N$ and the singleton clusters are not defined beside the display) and P032-N003 (the labels 111, …, 222 of Tables 2–4 are literally the dyads $(1,1)$, $(2,1)$, $(2,2)$, two of them self-dyads, for which the identity would drop the off-diagonal terms within a self-dyad; relabelling repairs the illustration). ‘For longitudinal data’ means that repeated observations $t$ of a dyad are allowed. The paper states the model as linear ‘to ease exposition’; for other estimators the same algebra applies to scores and bread (P032-T4). The sentence on square roots presupposes nonnegative diagonal entries (footnote 3; P032-T6, P032-T7). The sentence that follows on p. 191 (‘Limit theorems for dyadic data (Tabord-Meehan 2019) establish that DCRSEs may be used to form asymptotically valid confidence intervals and $p$-values under a normal approximation’) cites an external theorem and is not a target (P032-N014, not confirmed).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The positive-semidefinite option, corrected: eigenvalue clipping applied whenever the option is requested, whatever the signs of the diagonal, returns a positive semidefinite matrix
canonical_claim.location: p. 191 (PDF p. 6), footnote 3; R/dyad_funcs.R lines 70 and 155; dcr.ado lines 246–281
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol’s smallest repair (validated.json, P032-E005), verbatim: “When PSD enforcement is requested, run the eigenvalue clipping regardless of diagonal signs: for symmetric V=Q diag(lambda_j) Q^T return Q diag(max(lambda_j,0)) Q^T. In R replace the diagonal-sign gate with if (posdef == TRUE), and use diag(pos_eigens, nrow=length(pos_eigens)) to implement the formula for all parameter dimensions. In Stata remove the inner Indnegvar condition while retaining the outer psd condition and clipping block. No article-footnote correction is needed for the established defect.”
Formal content, with every hypothesis. Let $V$ be a real symmetric $p\times p$ matrix, $V = Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p)\,Q^T$ with $Q$ orthogonal, and $V_+ = Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\max(\lambda_1,0),\ldots,\max(\lambda_p,0))\,Q^T$.
(i) $V_+$ is symmetric and, for every $c\in\mathbb{R}^p$, $c^TV_+c = \sum_j\max(\lambda_j,0)(q_j^Tc)^2\ge0$, where $q_j$ is the $j$-th column of $Q$: $V_+$ is positive semidefinite.
(ii) $V_+ = V$ if and only if $V$ is positive semidefinite.
(iii) [A gate on the diagonal is not enough] A real symmetric matrix whose diagonal entries are all nonnegative need not be positive semidefinite: $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&d\end{pmatrix}$ with $a,d\ge0$ is positive semidefinite if and only if $ad\ge b^2$ (P032-T6 is an instance with $ad < b^2$). Hence the gated rule $\mathcal{G}$ of P032-T6 (e) returns a positive semidefinite matrix if and only if $V$ has a negative diagonal entry or $V$ is positive semidefinite, whereas $V\mapsto V_+$ always does.
(iv) [The example] For the matrix $V$ of P032-T6 (c), with $\tau = \mathrm{tr}\,V = \tfrac{467922}{3655808}$ and $\delta = \det V = -\tfrac{70529}{308915776}$, the eigenvalues are $\lambda_\pm = \tfrac12\big(\tau\pm\sqrt{\tau^2 - 4\delta}\big)$ with $\lambda_- < 0 < \lambda_+$, and $V_+ = \lambda_+qq^T$ for a unit eigenvector $q$ of $\lambda_+$: $V_+$ has rank one, $c^TV_+c\ge0$ for all $c$, and $V_+\ne V$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Footnote 3 and the software documentation, as printed: P032-T6. The spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices. In footnote 3 the inner quotation is the paper’s quotation of Cameron *et al.* (2011).
canonical_claim.note: Corrected statement for P032-E005 (error, Minor). Repair cost per the validator: none (no new assumption, same estimand); the repaired rule changes finite-sample variance estimates, diagonal entries included, in the cases newly corrected. The validator states that no correction to footnote 3 is needed and that no finite-sample inferential validity is claimed for the repaired matrix. (i) is in derivation.md, section 6, which also says that matrices already positive semidefinite, and matrices for which the present gate activates, come out the same under the repair ((ii)–(iii)); (iv) puts in exact form the validator’s numerical eigenvalues of the example (about $-0.00176$ and $0.12975$) and was computed when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2.1, ‘Toy Example: Bilateral Trade’: the variance of the average of two dyadic outcomes that share a member (two unnumbered displays), as printed
canonical_claim.location: pp. 188–189 (PDF pp. 3–4), Section 2.1, from ‘This clustering structure affects statistical inference’ to the end of the section
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed (p. 188): “This clustering structure affects statistical inference. To illustrate this, suppose we were interested in characterizing the variance of the average level of commerce between the US and the UK ($Y_{US-UK}$) and between the US and France ($Y_{US-FR}$). We can compute the sample mean of their outcomes: $\hat\mu = \frac12(Y_{US-UK} + Y_{US-FR})$. *If* we were to assume that dyads were statistically independent of one another, the variances are simply additive (i.e., there is no covariance term) and we could compute the variance of $\hat\mu$ as $$\mathrm{V}[\hat\mu]_{naive} = \mathrm{V}\Big[\frac12(Y_{US-UK} + Y_{US-FR})\Big] = \frac14\big(\mathrm{V}[Y_{US-UK}] + \mathrm{V}[Y_{US-FR}]\big).$$ However, with dyadic data, this may not be reasonable, especially when country-level factors are likely to impact dyadic outcomes. To see this, suppose that the true data-generating process is additive among countries, so that $$Y_{US,UK} = aX_{US} + bX_{UK} + U_{US,UK},$$ $$Y_{US,FR} = cX_{US} + dX_{FR} + U_{US,FR},$$ where the $X$ and the $U$ are independent, and all $X$ are pairwise-independent. In this instance, the true variance of $\hat\mu$ is”
As printed (p. 189): “$$\mathrm{V}[\hat\mu] = \mathrm{V}\Big[\frac12(Y_{US-UK} + Y_{US-FR})\Big] = \frac14\big(\mathrm{V}[Y_{US-UK}] + \mathrm{V}[Y_{US-FR}]\big) + \frac12\mathrm{Cov}[Y_{US-UK}, Y_{US-FR}]$$ $$= \mathrm{V}_{naive} + \frac12\mathrm{Cov}[aX_{US} + bX_{UK} + U_{US,UK}, cX_{US} + dX_{FR} + U_{US,FR}] = \mathrm{V}_{naive} + \frac{ac}{2}\mathrm{V}[X_{US}].$$ When $a$ and $c$ are of the same sign—that is, the dyads share a positive correlation—the naive characterization of the variance understates the true sampling variability. Our setting did not involve any “network effects” between countries: the problem emerges solely from the fact that a single country (here, the US) is, mechanically, present in more than one dyad in the data.”
Formal reading (exact). Let $X_{US}, X_{UK}, X_{FR}, U_{US,UK}, U_{US,FR}$ be real random variables with finite variances, $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}$, $Y_{US,UK} = aX_{US} + bX_{UK} + U_{US,UK}$, $Y_{US,FR} = cX_{US} + dX_{FR} + U_{US,FR}$, $\hat\mu = \tfrac12(Y_{US,UK} + Y_{US,FR})$ and $\mathrm{V}_{naive} = \tfrac14(\mathrm{V}[Y_{US,UK}] + \mathrm{V}[Y_{US,FR}])$.
(i) $\mathrm{V}[\hat\mu] = \mathrm{V}_{naive} + \tfrac12\mathrm{Cov}[Y_{US,UK},Y_{US,FR}]$ (no independence needed).
(ii) If the five variables are mutually independent (pairwise uncorrelated suffices), then $\mathrm{Cov}[Y_{US,UK},Y_{US,FR}] = ac\,\mathrm{V}[X_{US}]$ and $\mathrm{V}[\hat\mu] = \mathrm{V}_{naive} + \tfrac{ac}{2}\mathrm{V}[X_{US}]$.
(iii) Under the hypothesis of (ii), if $ac > 0$ and $\mathrm{V}[X_{US}] > 0$ then $\mathrm{V}_{naive} < \mathrm{V}[\hat\mu]$; if $ac < 0$ and $\mathrm{V}[X_{US}] > 0$ then $\mathrm{V}_{naive} > \mathrm{V}[\hat\mu]$; and if $ac = 0$ or $\mathrm{V}[X_{US}] = 0$ the two are equal.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat\mu$ and $\mathrm{V}[\hat\mu]_{naive}$ are defined in the quoted passage; ‘naive’ is the variance computed as if the two outcomes were uncorrelated. The paper writes the outcomes $Y_{US-UK}$, $Y_{US-FR}$ in the variance displays and $Y_{US,UK}$, $Y_{US,FR}$ in the model, and the naive variance both as $\mathrm{V}[\hat\mu]_{naive}$ and as $\mathrm{V}_{naive}$; each pair denotes one object. Table 1 (p. 188) illustrates the two dependence patterns and is not needed for the statement.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P032-H9, its formal half (the first sentence of the claim, on what repeated-dyad clustering misses, is expository). Both readers held the displays up. P032-N002 (not confirmed) records that if ‘the $X$ and the $U$ are independent’ is read only as independence of the $X$’s from the $U$’s, the last equality also needs $\mathrm{Cov}[U_{US,UK},U_{US,FR}] = 0$; on the natural reading (all five variables independent) the algebra is correct, which is why (ii) states the hypothesis explicitly. The paper’s ‘when $a$ and $c$ are of the same sign’ is the case $ac > 0$ of (iii), with $\mathrm{V}[X_{US}] > 0$ implicit; the opposite-sign case of (iii) is not stated in the paper and is included because the sign condition is what P032-E001 turns on (P032-T5). Finite variances are implicit in the paper.
